--- title: "4 · Fitting" subtitle: "Any regression method can be used: they all read the same two objects, A and b" --- ```{=html}
You needgram (A and b per genotype and year) from step 3.You getcoefficients from OLS, ridge, sparse (SSR) and lasso fits, and a feel for which terms matter.
``` ::: {.cell} ::: ## One pooled problem To start simply, pool **all genotypes and all years** into one regression. We add up the per-trajectory statistics and put every library column on a common scale (unit root-mean-square), so coefficient sizes are comparable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} st <- sum_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years)) # add up all years, keep genotypes apart A <- apply(st$A, c(2, 3), sum) # add up genotypes too b <- colSums(st$b) sc <- scale_gram(A, b, n = sum(st$n)) # scaled normal equations terms <- gram$names ``` ::: ## A fitting method is a function `fit(A, b, ...)` Every method takes the same two objects and returns `list(coef, support)`. ```r fit_ols <- function(A, b, ...) { list(coef = solve(A, b), support = seq_along(b)) } ``` ```r fit_ridge <- function(A, b, lambda = 0.01, ...) { list(coef = solve(A + lambda * mean(diag(A)) * diag(nrow(A)), b), support = seq_along(b)) } ``` ```r fit_ssr <- function(A, b, k = 8, alpha = 1e-6, ...) { S <- seq_along(b) repeat { co <- solve(A[S, S, drop = FALSE] + alpha * diag(length(S)), b[S]) if (length(S) <= k) break S <- S[-which.min(abs(co))] } coef <- numeric(length(b)); coef[S] <- co list(coef = coef, support = S) } ``` **Ordinary least squares** uses every term. **Ridge** shrinks them. **Sequential thresholding** (SSR) refits, removes the smallest coefficient, and repeats until $k$ terms remain. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ols <- fit_ols(sc$A, sc$b) rdg <- fit_ridge(sc$A, sc$b, lambda = 0.01) ssr <- fit_ssr(sc$A, sc$b, k = 8) tab <- data.frame(term = terms, OLS = ols$coef, ridge = rdg$coef, SSR_8 = ssr$coef) tab[, -1] <- round(tab[, -1], 3); tab ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` term OLS ridge SSR_8 1 1 0.156 0.143 0.154 2 TT -0.034 0.002 -0.016 3 TT^2 -0.032 -0.033 -0.030 4 TT^3 0.018 0.005 0.011 5 DL 0.019 -0.007 0.002 6 DL^2 -0.055 -0.040 -0.056 7 DL^3 0.024 0.020 0.026 8 RAW 0.011 0.009 0.000 9 RAW^2 -0.017 -0.015 -0.020 10 RAW^3 -0.001 0.002 0.000 11 RAD 0.007 0.008 0.000 12 RAD^2 -0.003 -0.003 0.000 13 RAD^3 -0.001 -0.002 0.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- reshape(tab, direction = "long", varying = list(2:4), v.names = "coef", timevar = "method", times = names(tab)[2:4], idvar = "term") d$term <- factor(d$term, rev(terms)); d$method <- factor(d$method, names(tab)[2:4]) ggplot(d, aes(coef, term, fill = method)) + geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.75) + scale_fill_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("blue", "cyan", "orange")])) + labs(x = "coefficient (scaled library)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme_dgxe() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](04-fitting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=1036.8} ::: ::: ## Watching the sparse fit decide SSR removes terms one at a time. The order shows what the data cannot do without: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} S <- seq_along(terms); out <- character(0) while (length(S) > 1) { co <- solve(sc$A[S, S, drop = FALSE] + 1e-6 * diag(length(S)), sc$b[S]) w <- which.min(abs(co)); out <- c(out, terms[S[w]]); S <- S[-w] } data.frame(removed_in_order = out, terms_left_after = 12:1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` removed_in_order terms_left_after 1 RAW^3 12 2 RAD^3 11 3 RAD^2 10 4 RAD 9 5 RAW 8 6 DL 7 7 TT^3 6 8 TT 5 9 RAW^2 4 10 DL^3 3 11 DL^2 2 12 TT^2 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(last_standing = terms[S]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` last_standing "1" ``` ::: ::: The first terms to go are the high powers of radiation and water, and what survives longest are the constant and the powers of thermal time and day length. Be careful with this ranking: it is not an importance measure. A term can be dropped because its effect is shared with correlated powers of the same driver, and the order depends on the library. The honest question is how many terms the model needs to predict well on unseen years, which is the topic of step 5; step 6 then reads the fitted *curves* rather than individual coefficients. ## Writing your own method: lasso in ten lines Nothing above is special. Any method that turns `(A, b)` into coefficients works. As an example, the lasso written as coordinate descent on the same scaled normal equations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_lasso <- function(A, b, lambda = 0.01, iters = 2000, ...) { xi <- numeric(length(b)) for (it in seq_len(iters)) { old <- xi for (j in seq_along(b)) { r <- b[j] - sum(A[j, -j] * xi[-j]) # partial residual xi[j] <- sign(r) * max(abs(r) - lambda, 0) / A[j, j] # soft threshold } if (max(abs(xi - old)) < 1e-9) break } list(coef = xi, support = which(xi != 0)) } las <- fit_lasso(sc$A, sc$b, lambda = 2e-4) setNames(round(las$coef, 3), terms) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 TT TT^2 TT^3 DL DL^2 DL^3 RAW RAW^2 RAW^3 RAD 0.149 0.000 -0.034 0.004 -0.003 -0.045 0.023 0.010 -0.017 0.000 0.005 RAD^2 RAD^3 -0.003 0.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Idea"} The method is a **plug-in**. Steps 2 and 3 produced `A` and `b`; step 4 turns them into coefficients; steps 5 to 8 only need `coef` and `support`. Replace the fitting function and nothing else changes. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Check"} OLS and ridge should be close (the problem is well conditioned). Sparse fits should agree with OLS on the terms they keep. If a sparse fit changes sign on a large coefficient, the library has collinear terms. ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Swap"} Try `fit_ssr(sc$A, sc$b, k = 5)`, `fit_ridge(..., lambda = 1)`, or `fit_lasso(..., lambda = 1e-3)`. The next step shows how to judge them honestly: on years the model has never seen. :::
